## Decision requested

Approve a documented traffic-flow exception under **SC-7(4)** exempting the
Microsoft 365 **Optimize** endpoint set from TLS break-and-inspect at branch
direct-internet egress, for the *[N]* pilot sites listed at Attachment A.

The controls the exception punctures are named at clause 3. One of them —
tenant restrictions v2 — cannot be re-established at the network layer once the
proxy is bypassed and has to be re-signaled from the endpoint; clause 4 states
how, and what it does not cover. Compensating controls are at clause 6 and the
reversal commitments at clause 7.
:::

## 1. Background

Microsoft 365 Informed Network Routing, which supplies Microsoft's
network-quality signal to SD-WAN path selection, is not available to GCC
Moderate tenants. Microsoft states this directly in its product documentation,
and the agency's own substrate encodes it as a machine-enforced contract
fixture — **FINDING-001** — so the constraint is designed for rather than
missed. Commercial and sovereign cloud feature parity is sequenced rather than
simultaneous; the capability is absent from all five of the non-commercial
clouds Microsoft names.

The agency's Catalyst SD-WAN fabric will therefore steer Microsoft 365 traffic
using Cloud OnRamp for SaaS probe measurements alone, with local direct
internet access at branch sites. This is a product-availability limitation in
the government cloud, not a FedRAMP or authorization boundary matter, and it
requires no FedRAMP action.

## 2. What is being sought: an SC-7(4) traffic-flow exception

This is **not** a general risk acceptance. It is a **documented traffic-flow
exception under SC-7(4)**, and it carries that control's discipline: a named
exception with its supporting mission need, reviewed on a stated cadence, with
the SD-WAN steering log serving as the *enforcement evidence* that the
exception's boundaries hold.

The distinction matters at assessment. **Documentation alone is not a
compensating control.** What makes the carve-out defensible is that the DPI
classification steering an Optimize flow around the overlay is itself a logged,
per-flow record of which traffic rests on application-layer encryption and
which rides the tunnel.

## 3. Controls affected, named

Traffic to Microsoft 365 Optimize endpoints will egress locally at pilot branch
sites without traversing the campus policy enforcement point. Naming what that
punctures, rather than describing it as "inspection forgone":

- **SI-3** — no secure web gateway inline malicious-code inspection on the
  bypassed flows.
- **SI-4(10)** — no visibility into the content of encrypted communications.
  The TLS break-and-inspect that satisfies this control for proxied flows is
  absent by design here.
- **AC-4** — no CASB information-flow enforcement on those flows.
- **AU-3, and AU-12 by reference** — records are still generated for the
  bypassed flows, so what degrades is their *content*: five-tuple plus steering
  metadata over encrypted media, not user, device, application, action and data
  type. AU-12 requires generation with the content AU-3 defines, so naming AU-3
  states the degradation precisely.

**SC-8 is explicitly not a gap**, and the memo says so to forestall the obvious
challenge. Optimize flows carry their own FIPS-validated encryption — TLS, and
SRTP for Teams media — and the IPsec overlay continues to encrypt every flow
that does not. This is the per-flow closure the coverage doctrine already
concedes, not a new hole.

This follows Microsoft's published connectivity guidance, which recommends
bypassing inspection for these endpoints because they are secured at the client
and service ends and because re-encrypting inspected traffic introduces
protocol errors and risk of its own. The agency is implementing the vendor's
documented design, not departing from it.

## 4. The control that moves off the network path: tenant restrictions

**Tenant-to-tenant exfiltration over an Optimize-categorized path** is the case
an assessor will construct against this exemption, and it should be answered in
the record rather than discovered at assessment.

The answer is that tenant restrictions v2 does not depend on the proxy.
[Microsoft documents three enforcement
paths](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/external-id/tenant-restrictions-v2)
for a single cross-tenant access policy, and proxy header injection is the
weakest of them: it signals at the *authentication plane only* and does not
reach the data plane. The agency therefore does not lose this control by
bypassing the proxy — it re-signals it from the endpoint, where the coverage is
better than what the proxy provided.

| Path | Proxy required | Authentication plane | Data plane |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Windows Group Policy** on corporate-owned devices | No | Yes | **Yes** |
| Universal tenant restrictions (Global Secure Access) | No | Yes, all platforms | Graph only |
| Corporate proxy header injection | Yes | Yes | **No** |

- **Windows Group Policy signaling** on corporate-owned devices — no proxy
  required, and the only path that carries *both* authentication-plane and
  data-plane protection. Policy evaluation remains in the cloud; the device
  supplies the signal. With the proxy given up and Global Secure Access
  unavailable in this cloud, **this is not the agency's preferred path but its
  only one**.
- **Universal tenant restrictions via Global Secure Access** — authentication
  plane on every operating system, browser and form factor, and data plane for
  Microsoft Graph only. **Not available to this agency:** Global Secure Access
  is non-FIPS in GCC Moderate and unavailable in GCC High and DoD. Recorded so
  the option reads as closed rather than untried.
- **Proxy header injection** — the path being given up, and the one the
  exemption removes. Authentication plane only.

That leaves one path, which raises the stakes on its limits — so they are
stated rather than glossed. The Group Policy path covers Office applications,
Universal Windows Platform .NET applications and Microsoft Edge; non-Edge
browsers and non-Windows devices are not covered by it, and any such population
at a pilot site is in scope for the exemption but not for this compensating
control. Parts of tenant restrictions v2 remain in preview. **This control is
therefore compensable but not automatically compensated:** it is in force only
if the device-side signaling is configured and verified before cutover, which
clause 6 records as a precondition and clause 8 as a return trigger.

## 5. Scope, and why it is bounded

- **Endpoints:** the Optimize category only, enumerated from the Microsoft 365
  IP and URL web service, `Instance=Worldwide` — the instance serving GCC. The
  Allow and Default categories are *not* in scope and remain subject to
  existing inspection.
- **Change control:** the set is machine-readable and published, with additions
  released 30 days before they become active. Scope is reviewed on the feed's
  monthly update cadence — which is also the SC-7(4) review cadence.
- **Sites:** the pilot sites at Attachment A only, recorded per circuit rather
  than per site. Fleet expansion is not authorized by this memo.
- **Architecture:** classified under TIC 3.0 as Branch Office to Cloud Service
  Provider. Architecture review sign-off at Attachment B.

## 6. Compensating controls, by plane

Each of these is named because the network can no longer see what it covers.
**A control listed here without a reference is not yet a compensating control.**

- **Identity plane** — Conditional Access on the affected services, and a
  cross-tenant access policy with tenant restrictions v2 signaled from the
  endpoint per clause 4. **Precondition to cutover:** device-side signaling
  configured and verified at every pilot site, with the uncovered device and
  browser population enumerated — *[policy references; GPO or Intune
  configuration; uncovered population]*.
- **Service plane** — Defender for Office 365 and Purview DLP for content the
  network cannot inspect — *[policies in force]*.
- **Endpoint** — EDR and endpoint DLP on managed devices, which see the content
  after decryption — *[EDR / configuration baseline]*.
- **Evidence** — the SD-WAN steering log as SC-7(4) enforcement evidence, plus
  branch policy enforcement point telemetry reaching CISA's Cloud Log
  Aggregation Warehouse under reporting pattern *[reference]*. This is the
  AU-12 contract for the SD-WAN layer.
- **Path assurance** — Cisco ThousandEyes for Government (FedRAMP Moderate
  authorized), with pre-cutover baselines captured at every pilot site, and
  agents verified as registered to the government instance.

## 7. Reversal

Steering reverts per site within one shift by network operations, without an
approval cycle. Reversion returns traffic to backhaul through the campus policy
enforcement point, restoring the prior enforcement posture rather than
degrading it.

Withdrawal of the exception is a tracked step of any such rollback. The agency
commits that the exception will not remain in force at sites returned to
backhaul — leaving it in place would retain the accepted risk while forfeiting
the performance it was accepted for.

## 8. Return to the Authorizing Official

The system owner will return for a further decision if: the exception scope
widens beyond the Optimize category; sites are added outside Attachment A; a
compensating control named above is found not to be in place, including tenant
restrictions v2 device-side signaling at a site being cut over; the SC-7(4)
review finds the steering log no longer evidences the exception's boundaries;
or the exception is withdrawn during a rollback.

## 9. Matters not yet confirmed

Disclosed for completeness; none blocks this decision, and each is tracked to
closure:

- Whether ThousandEyes Enterprise Agents hosted on Catalyst routers can
  register to the government platform instance. Standalone agent deployment is
  the fallback and does not affect this exception.
- Microsoft publishes no rationale for the GCC limitation. None is required for
  this decision — the limitation is documented and the exception does not rest
  on why it exists.
- **Cisco and ThousandEyes material was accessed indirectly** and is being
  reconfirmed against current versions, as is the TIC 3.0 Reference
  Architecture. Microsoft documentation and the TIC 3.0 Security Capabilities
  Catalog were both read from source; Attachment B's capability-group list is
  verified against catalog v3.3.
